mech: Each rice delta or river valley could feed a dynasty, and the forest, hill and dry belts between them made holding more than two or three cores very costly.
With trade and coinage shrinking, kings paid priests and officials with villages and their revenue instead of cash.
Grants alienated revenue, justice and policing to intermediaries, so sovereignty was parcelled out in layers and no centre could pull it back.

view: B.D. Chattopadhyaya and Hermann Kulke (integrative state formation)
mech: Grants planted Brahmin settlements and temples on agrarian frontiers, drawing tribes and local chiefs into new regional kingdoms: integration from below, not feudal decay.
With the Gupta overlordship gone and Harsha's empire dying with him in 647, power settled in regional dynasties rather than a new pan-Indian one.
Three regional powers of similar strength fought for Kanauj, the symbolic seat of northern overlordship; each could win it, none could keep it.
A century of war with Palas and Rashtrakutas drained the Pratiharas, who were already shrinking when Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Kanauj in 1018.
The shared ideal of the universal king (cakravartin) was met by ritual conquest, tribute and Sanskrit praise, so regional kings could claim the whole world without annexing it.
Because caste ranked priests above kings and castes ran village life, dynasties changed without touching society and few subjects had stakes in a large state.
Brahmadeya villages and temple endowments formed the nodes through which Chola kings tied themselves to peasant localities.
Gifts to temples bought ritual precedence over the nadus, which kept their own assemblies, so the king's real reach beyond the Kaveri core stayed thin.
A hegemony held by ritual prestige rather than officials dissolved when Pandya and Hoysala rivals out-gave and out-fought the Cholas.
Temple accounts and land surveys show a revenue state able to fund fleets across the Bay of Bengal, more than a ritual hegemony could do.
Horse-rich Turkic armies based in the dry uplands of Afghanistan rode down an open corridor into the Punjab plains each winter.
Ghaznavid Lahore became a Persianate base on Indian soil from which the Ghurids later conquered the Ganges plain.
Command of the arid frontier's horses and cavalry archers let a slave general's army take and hold the north Indian plain.
To pay a standing cavalry big enough to stop the Mongols, Alauddin Khalji assessed the Doab at half the crop in cash and fixed market prices.
A centre able to tax hard was tempted to stretch across the Deccan, but distance meant governors there had armies and revenue of their own.
Revolts in the Deccan produced Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmani sultanate (1347): the south never returned to Delhi.
Timur emptied Delhi's treasury and armies; Gujarat, Malwa and Jaunpur governors crowned themselves within a decade.
A north split between rival sultans and Rajput kings could not combine against an invader, as Babur himself observed.
Babur's field guns and matchlocks behind a wagon barricade broke Ibrahim Lodi's elephants.
Mounted archers wheeling round the flanks, the arid zone's old weapon, did as much as the guns; Mughal power stayed a cavalry power.
Silver imports let Mughal mints strike enough rupees for land revenue to be assessed and paid in coin.
Cash revenue made rotating assignments workable: a noble could be moved to any province because his pay came as a sum, not a lordship.
Ranks, cash salaries and transfers every few years kept the nobility dependent on the emperor, the first durable answer to India's centrifugal pull.
Abolishing the poll tax on non-Muslims signalled that Hindu warrior lineages could be partners, not subjects.
The most formidable warrior clans of the north became Mughal generals and in-laws, turning a likely resistance into an imperial army.
Like China, South Asia was an exposed zone: its largest empires were built by conquerors from the Inner Asian frontier, whose cohesion and horses outmatched agrarian rivals.
Aurangzeb besieged and annexed Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda the next year.
The eight-month siege of Golconda ended the last independent Deccan sultanate.
The conquests carried the empire to its greatest extent, almost to the far south.
Any governor with cash could hire Afghan and Rajput soldiers from the open military labour market and defy the centre.
Deccani peasant-soldiers with light horses gave Shivaji and the Peshwas a cheap, mobile army that Mughal heavy cavalry could not pin down.
The Company won India with Indian soldiers hired from the same market, drilled and, crucially, paid regularly.
Nayaka chiefs with their own armies and lands became the kings of Madurai, Thanjavur and Mysore once the centre lost at Talikota.
The rout and the sack of the capital by the allied sultans broke the core the nayakas had served.
A revenue machine that paid an army that won more revenue: by 1818 no Indian power could field a match.
Indian bankers and revenue farmers backed the Company because it paid its debts and protected trade: the conquest rode on Indian capital.
Jagirdars moved every few years had no reason to protect the peasants of an estate they would soon leave, so they took all they could.
Peasants fled or took up arms under zamindar leaders when the demand left too little to live on.
To win over Deccani and Maratha nobles Aurangzeb handed out high ranks, but Deccan jagirs yielded little: too many claimants, not enough paying land.
Assignments in rebel districts could not be collected, shrinking the pool of paying jagirs.
Nobles short of good jagirs formed factions around princes and wazirs to control the assignment office.
Reimposing the jizya and destroying temples turned Hindu subjects, Rajputs and Marathas against the dynasty.
A generation of war wrecked the Deccan economy and trained Maratha captains to raid Mughal territory and tax it.
Marathas took a share of Mughal revenue through the empire's own institutions, and governors cut deals with them that loosened Delhi's hold.
A weak and contested throne could not move governors at will; Murshid Quli Khan in Bengal and Saadat Khan in Awadh stayed put and founded dynasties.

view: Muzaffar Alam and C.A. Bayly (regional revival)
mech: Provincial zamindars and merchants grew rich enough to back governors who kept more revenue at home: decline at the centre was growth at the edges.
A century of cash revenue and silver built market towns, bankers and service gentry in the provinces.
Nader Shah carried off the treasury and the Peacock Throne; after 1739 no governor feared Delhi.
Regional courts farmed revenue to bankers and merchants, who grew into the "portfolio capitalists" of the age.
Bengal's rich, autonomous nawabi court was a prize, and its bankers and generals were willing to change sides.
Victory let the Company install its own nawab and draw on Bengal's revenue to pay its armies.
Defeating the Mughal emperor, Awadh and Bengal together at Buxar forced Shah Alam to grant the diwani.
Legal control of Bengal's land revenue gave the Company a tax base to fight the Marathas and Mysore.
The Afghan rout of the Marathas removed the one power that might have reunited the north just as the Company rose in Bengal.
From 1803 the emperor was a Company pensioner in Delhi.
Rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II their emperor; after Delhi fell the British tried and exiled him.
Silk and wool weavers rioted against Indian calicoes; Parliament banned printed imports in 1700 and their use in 1721.
A home market shut to Indian prints became a protected nursery for British cotton imitators.
Indian cloth set the price and quality to beat, pushing British makers to invent machines that could spin fine strong cotton yarn.
Steam power freed mills from rivers and multiplied the spindles one worker could tend.
British yarn and cloth prices fell by more than half, undercutting Indian spinning above all.
Dearer grain raised the money wage weavers needed, so India lost its cost edge in cloth even before Lancashire's machines matured.
Mughal fragmentation brought wars, tolls and insecurity that cut farm output and raised grain prices.
Repeated droughts cut harvests and pushed grain prices to famine levels across south and west India.
The north Indian famine of 1783-84 drove grain prices sharply up.

view: Romesh Chunder Dutt and Amiya Bagchi
mech: Company agents forced Bengal weavers to take advances and sell below market, while British tariffs shut out Indian cloth.
After 1813 Manchester cloth entered India at low duties while Indian cloth paid high duties in Britain.
Displaced spinners and weavers fell back on the land; in Gangetic Bihar the share of people in industry roughly halved over the 19th century.
The ruin of the weavers became the founding story of Indian economic nationalism.
Bengal's revenue, not British silver, now paid for the Company's exports of cloth and its China tea: a transfer without return.
Naoroji built his "drain" from the official figures for remittances to London.
To remit the home charges India had to run an export surplus, which helped close Britain's deficits with America and Europe.
Much of the home charges was guaranteed interest on London capital that built railways and pensions for an army and civil service: payment for services, not pure tribute.
The drain argument gave the boycott of British cloth its economic logic.

view: Morris D. Morris and Tirthankar Roy
mech: Imported British spinning machinery let Bombay capitalists industrialise cotton on Indian soil.
Railways cut freight costs by around four-fifths, tying inland farms to ports and world prices.
The canal halved the voyage to Europe and made Indian wheat and oilseeds competitive there.
Irrigated Punjab became an export granary of wheat and cotton.
The failed rains of 1769 destroyed the main rice crop of Bengal and Bihar.
The Company had promised London a rising surplus from the diwani and kept collecting.
Full revenue demands and grain speculation by Company servants left peasants nothing to fall back on.
Depopulation and failing collections convinced reformers that a fixed, permanent demand would revive cultivation.
An extreme El Nino failed the monsoon over the Deccan and the south in 1876 and again in 1877.
Officials believed relief would demoralise the poor and that private trade would feed the hungry better than the state.
Grain left famine districts for export while the Temple ration of 1 lb of grain a day for hard labour starved relief workers.
Cotton and export crops replaced village grain reserves and tied peasants to falling world prices and moneylenders.
Railways moved grain out of drought districts to central depots where prices were higher.
The scandal of 1876-78 produced the Famine Commission of 1880 and the codes that followed.
The 1896 monsoon failed across central and northern India.
The 1899 monsoon was the driest of the 19th century in western and central India.
Hunger turned endemic malaria into a killer when the rains returned.
Most deaths of 1899-1901 came with the malaria and cholera that followed starvation.
Once a district was on the railway, rainfall shocks raised its death rate much less: grain could flow in.
Early declarations of scarcity and relief works paying in cash kept labourers able to buy food.
The collapse in Malaya let Japan overrun Burma within months.
Bengal lost Burmese rice imports, a small but price-setting share of supply.
Rice prices rose several-fold while wages of labourers, fishermen and artisans barely moved: they could no longer buy food.
Food availability in 1943 was not exceptionally low; people starved because they lost the means to command it.

view: Mark Tauger and S.Y. Padmanabhan (food availability decline)
mech: The cyclone and brown spot fungus cut the 1942 aman crop far more than official figures showed: there really was a shortage.
Seizing boats destroyed fishermen's and boatmen's livelihoods and the rice trade of the delta.
Wheat that could have broken the price spiral was kept for war stocks and Europe.
Priority for the war effort and Calcutta, plus denial of the scale of shortage, turned scarcity into mass death: a war famine.
Excess deaths peaked in late 1943 and 1944 from malaria, cholera and smallpox, after starvation had weakened survivors.
The new dynasty built its own capital in Iraq, between the Persian east that backed it and the Syrian west it had beaten.
A Khurasani dynasty ruling from old Sasanian land adopted Persian imperial ideas to rule Persian elites.
Sasanian lore held that Persian kings had gathered the sciences scattered by Alexander; Abbasid caliphs funded translation to play that role, and courtiers, doctors and astrologers kept demand going.
Paper made in Baghdad from the 790s made books and bureaucratic records cheap enough to copy by the thousand.
Iraq's farm revenues and Gulf trade made Baghdad rich enough for lavish patrons.
Al-Kindi and al-Farabi worked from the translated Aristotle and Plato.
The House of Wisdom was a palace library in the Sasanian tradition; the translations were paid for by many patrons, not one academy.
The caliphs' attempt to impose a theology failed against Ibn Hanbal and the scholars; after 848 doctrine belonged to the ulama.
Al-Mu'tasim's Turkish slave guards owed loyalty to their commanders and their pay; when it ran short they killed caliphs.
Fourteen years of war wrecked the date groves and canals of southern Iraq and sacked Basra in 871.
Paying the army consumed the revenue, provinces stopped remitting, and by 936 the caliph handed power to a military amir.
The shrinking yield of Iraq's irrigated land, the caliphate's fiscal heart, left the caliphs unable to pay soldiers.
Short of cash, the Buyids paid their Daylami and Turkish troops with assignments of land tax.

view: Robert McC. Adams and Peter Christensen
mech: Assignees held land briefly and had no interest in maintaining the canals that kept it fertile.
Repeated hard winters killed the cotton crop and brought famine to Khurasan's cotton towns.
Cold drove Turkmen herders south into Iran and Iraq, and famine weakened the cities they took.
Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk built endowed colleges to train Sunni jurists against Ismaili rivals.
Al-Ghazali wrote the Incoherence while chief professor at the Baghdad Nizamiyya.

view: Older orientalist view, criticised by Saliba and Griffel
mech: Ghazali's attack on the philosophers supposedly turned Muslims against reason and science.
Madrasas taught law and religion; the "foreign sciences" lacked autonomous, corporate institutions like Europe's universities.
Islamic science stayed creative until the 16th century; it slowed when Atlantic and Cape trade drew wealth away from its patrons.
Al-Tusi and his circle's non-Ptolemaic models were carried forward by Ibn al-Shatir and the Samarkand school.
Partnerships died with a partner and estates were split among many heirs, so firms never grew large or permanent; Europe built the corporation instead.
Capital locked in endowments under fixed founders' terms could not move to new uses or form self-governing bodies.
Slave armies made rulers independent of local elites, so no assembly or nobility bound the ruler, and coups were easy.
Without parliaments that bargained taxes for rights, Muslim states built fewer limits on rulers.

view: Jared Rubin; Cosgel, Miceli and Rubin
mech: Sultans needed the legitimacy religious scholars and scribes provided, so they did not override their interest against Arabic-script printing.
Two and a half centuries without the press slowed the spread of literacy, commerce and new ideas.
Open markets turned the empire into a raw-material exporter; the real divergence came in the 19th century.
Losing perhaps a third of its people, Egypt and Syria saw urban real wages rise for a few generations, as in Europe.
Merchants and rulers moved Indian and Persian crops west along the caliphate's routes.
With Iran conquered, the Mongols sent Hulagu west to finish the Ismailis and bring the caliph to heel.
Hulagu executed al-Musta'sim and ended five centuries of Abbasid rule in Baghdad.
Libraries were sacked with the city; how many books were lost, and the story of the Tigris running black with ink, are later embellishments.
Massacre, flight and broken dykes cut Iraq's population sharply.

view: Robert McC. Adams and Peter Christensen
mech: Settlement surveys show the Diyala plains emptying for centuries before 1258; the Mongols struck a system already failing.
Baybars installed a surviving Abbasid as caliph in Cairo to crown Mamluk rule.
Victory over the Mongols made the Mamluks the defenders of Islam, and a caliph confirmed it.
Hulagu funded al-Tusi's observatory a year after sacking Baghdad.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: The sack is often said to have ended the golden age of Islamic science.
With Baghdad gone the Gulf route faded further and Mamluk Egypt's Red Sea route won the India trade.

view: Omer Lutfi Barkan (as weighed by Sevket Pamuk)
mech: American silver reaching the Levant through Europe drove prices up.
More coins with less silver, rising monetisation and faster circulation explain more of the price rise than imported silver alone.
The cost of musketeers in the long Habsburg and Safavid wars outran revenue; the mint was the quickest fix.
Peasants armed as musketeers (sekban) were dismissed after campaigns and turned bandit.
The 1590s were among the coldest years of the Little Ice Age, with drought and frost across the eastern Mediterranean.
Crop failure and livestock deaths, on top of wartime requisitions, pushed villagers into the rebel bands.
Contemporaries called it the Great Flight: whole districts were abandoned.
Rather than fight every rebel, Istanbul made bandit leaders governors, keeping them dependent and divided.
Cash-hungry armies needed tax farms that paid up front; in 1695 they were sold for life.
Life-term tax farmers and their local agents became the provincial notables who ran the 18th-century empire.
Killing a sultan who tried to replace the janissaries showed that the army and jurists, not the dynasty alone, now decided.
Monetisation let commoners buy into the janissary corps and tax farming, widening the political class.
The sultans' long fight to escape their constraints ended in 1826, when Mahmud II restored absolutism by destroying the janissaries.
Venal offices, provincial magnates and a hidebound elite let the state fall behind Europe.
Defeat at Vienna opened sixteen years of Holy League war that ended with the loss of Hungary.
The first great cession began a century of mostly defensive wars.
Crushing defeats by Russia proved the old army could not win, spurring Selim III's and then Mahmud II's new troops.
An army raised through notables and unpaid irregulars met a Russian army of drilled conscripts.
With the janissaries gone the palace could centralise and reform the law.
Four decades of reform built the bureaucrats who wrote the 1876 constitution.
Facing British imports, Ottoman producers shifted to cheaper labour, rural workshops and export lines like carpets, rather than vanishing.
Men of the old timar and palace order lamented a "decline" that was really their own displacement by new soldiers and tax farmers.
Creditor control of revenues narrowed the state's room for manoeuvre before the wars that ended it.
Barays and canals stored and spread monsoon water over a vast low-density city of rice fields.
Feeding and building for hundreds of thousands stripped the forests of the Kulen hills.
Eroded soil silted canals and reservoirs.
Decades-long droughts in the mid-14th and early 15th centuries left the system unable to deliver water.
Intense monsoons between droughts scoured channels and breached embankments; failures cascaded through the linked network.
As water control failed, the dense urban core lost its reason and means to stay.
A religion of monks and village temples drained the ideology and labour that had built the royal temple city.
The new Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya raided Angkor repeatedly and in 1431 took it.
After the Thai capture the court abandoned Angkor for the south.
Elites had been leaving the core for decades before 1431; the sack sealed a move already under way.
Booming maritime trade with China made the Mekong-Tonle Sap confluence more valuable than the rice plain of Angkor.

view: Alison Carter and Dan Penny (critics of the lost-city myth)
mech: A shrunken but never empty site, with Angkor Wat still a working monastery, let French writers imagine a vanished race.
Rising Chinese and European demand for pepper, cloves and nutmeg built rich, outward-looking port states.
Port rulers joined the faith of the Muslim merchant networks that brought them trade and allies.
Portuguese conquest scattered Muslim traders to Aceh, Johor, Banten and Brunei, spreading Islam with them.
The VOC used its charter and cannon to take Batavia (1619), Banda (1621), Malacca (1641) and Makassar (1669).
Monopoly contracts and conquest stripped Southeast Asian port states of their spice trade and their merchant class.
A cooler hemisphere weakened the Asian monsoon in the 17th century.
Drought and poor harvests compounded the commercial slump, as in the global crisis elsewhere.
Coastal trade revenue paid for Portuguese guns and gunners.
Firearms favoured the richest centres and helped Toungoo, Ayutthaya and the Nguyen absorb smaller rivals.
Trade, literacy and religious reform worked with agrarian growth to integrate the mainland, in a rhythm shared with France, Russia and Japan, and with no general 17th-century collapse.
Tax-free gifts to the sangha drained the crown's land and labour base, much as Indian land grants did.
Mongol invasions finished a kingdom already weakened from within.
The raid broke Srivijaya's grip on the strait, though the polity lingered for two more centuries.
The reversing monsoon set sailing seasons from the Gulf to India and on to China.
As Iraq decayed and Fatimid Egypt rose, the India trade moved from the Gulf to the Red Sea.
Aden became the hinge between Cairo's merchants and the Malabar coast.
Portuguese violence at Calicut drew a Mamluk-Gujarati fleet, which the Portuguese destroyed at Diu.
With no rival fleet left, the Portuguese could sell protection: passes for Asian ships.
Malacca, Goa and Hormuz gave the Portuguese the chokepoints to enforce their passes.
Asian and Muslim shippers evaded the blockade and Venice bought Red Sea pepper again in the 1560s.
Passes were a toll Asian merchants paid and routed around; the structures of Indian Ocean trade survived the Portuguese.
Companies that produced their own protection and planned whole voyages undercut the peddlers and caravans of the Levant route.
American silver flowed east because Asia valued it more; much of it ended in India and China.
The companies paid for cloth, pepper and saltpetre largely in bullion: Europe had little else India wanted.
Demand for Indian cloth drew bullion in: "bullion for goods".
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: The collapse of Safavid Iran (and trouble in Ottoman and Mughal hinterlands) cost Surat's shipowners their Gulf and Red Sea markets.
Mughal disorder cut Surat off from its inland markets and protection.
As Asian shipping shrank, British private traders out of Bombay and Calcutta took the routes.
Political power in Bengal gave British shipping privileged access to the most productive coast in Asia.
The voyage opened a direct sea route from Lisbon to India.

sources.cite: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 1898
